The baker opens the shop before the sun is up. She lights the oven first, because the oven takes the longest to wake, and then she turns to the dough that has been resting through the night. The dough is simple: flour, water, salt and a little of yesterday's starter. What makes it bread rather than paste is time. Over the night the yeast has eaten some of the sugar in the flour and breathed out gas, and the gas is trapped in a web of gluten that the baker built the evening before by folding the dough over and over on itself.

She cuts the dough into pieces and weighs each one. A loaf that is too heavy will not bake through; a loaf that is too light will burn at the edges before the middle is done. The scale is old and the numbers on it are worn, but she trusts it more than her hands. Each piece is shaped into a round, the surface pulled tight so that it will hold its form in the oven, and set seam side up in a basket lined with cloth.

By the time the first customers arrive, the shop smells of crust. The first customer is always the same man, who buys two loaves and a newspaper and asks about the weather. The baker tells him that it will rain later in the day, which is what she tells him every morning, and on most mornings she is right. The second customer is a student who counts coins carefully on the counter and buys whatever is cheapest. The baker sometimes adds a roll to the bag without saying anything.

The work of the shop has a rhythm that does not change much from season to season. In winter the dough rises slowly and she keeps it near the oven; in summer it rises too fast and she keeps it in the cold room at the back. In autumn there are apples, and she bakes a tart that sells out before noon. In spring there is nothing special, and she bakes the same bread she always bakes, and people buy it anyway.

People sometimes ask her why she does not make more kinds of bread. There are shops in the city that sell twenty kinds, with seeds and nuts and fruit and flours from grains that most people have never heard of. She says that she would rather make one thing well than twenty things badly, and that the people who come to her shop come for the one thing. This is mostly true. It is also true that she does not have room for twenty kinds of bread, and that she is tired by the end of the day.

The town around the shop is small. There is a river that runs through the middle of it, a bridge that crosses the river, a church on one side and a school on the other. The river floods every few years, and when it does the water comes up the street as far as the shop's front step and then, for reasons nobody has ever explained, stops. The baker's grandfather built the step. He said that he had measured the highest flood anyone could remember and added a hand's width, and so far the hand's width has been enough.

In the afternoon, when the bread is gone and the shelves are empty, the baker cleans. She scrapes the tables, sweeps the flour from the floor, and washes the baskets and the cloths. Then she mixes the dough for the next day. She measures the flour and the water by weight, never by volume, because a cup of flour can weigh more or less depending on how it is packed, and the difference shows in the bread. She adds the starter and the salt, and she folds the dough, and she folds it again, and she leaves it to rest.

There is a notebook on the shelf above the sink in which she writes down every batch: the date, the weight of the flour, the temperature of the room, how long the dough rested, and how the bread turned out. The notebook goes back eleven years. On the first page, in her handwriting from when she was younger, it says that the bread was too dense and that the crust was pale. On the most recent page it says that the bread was good. Most of the pages in between say something similar to one or the other, and a few of them say that something went wrong and she does not know why.

She has thought about what she would do if she ever stopped baking. She could travel, perhaps, or learn to paint, or simply sleep past four in the morning for the first time in years. But when she imagines the town without the smell of bread in the morning, she finds that she cannot picture it, and so she keeps the oven lit and the notebook open, and she writes down the numbers, one batch after another, and waits to see how the bread turns out.

On the last day of the year the shop is closed, and the baker walks along the river to the bridge and back. The water is high and brown and fast. She stands on the bridge for a while and watches it go, and then she walks home, and in the evening she mixes the dough for the first day of the new year, because the first customers will come early, as they always do, and they will want bread.
